en: The Hymn of One Hundred and Eight Names of Gaurī.
Now begins the hymn of one hundred and eight names of Gaurī.

**The Description of the Instruction on the Hymn of One Hundred and Eight Names of Gaurī by Dattātreya** 1. Having heard this meritorious narrative, variegated by the heroic power of Gaurī, Bhārgava again questioned the great sage Dattātreya. 2. "O Blessed One, the most wonderful heroic power of Gaurī has been recounted; indeed, there is no satiety for me as I listen to the story issuing from your mouth. 3. [He asked: "That hymn of one hundred and eight names of Gaurī which Bṛhaspati recited to Śacī..."

"Tell that to me, for my mind is exceedingly eager to hear it. (3) Thus questioned by the descendant of Bhṛgu, the king of yogis, the son of Atri, a treasury of compassion, recited the one hundred and eight names of Gaurī. (4) "O son of Jamadagni, listen to this hymn marked with the names of Gaurī; it is heart-captivating, bestows desired objects, and wards off great calamities. (5) The seer of this hymn is said to be Aṅgiras; the meter is declared to be Anuṣṭubh; and the deity is Gaurī. Whoever chants this for the sake of relief from distress—" (6)
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) with *hrāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and so forth, and having meditated, one should recite the hymn of praise.

One should meditate upon Gaurī, the bestower of desired objects, who is seated upon a lion, possesses a dark-blue luster, is adorned with saffron-colored garments, holds a sword, a shield, a trident, and a mallet in her hands, has the moon as her crest-jewel, and possesses three eyes.

Gaurī, the mother of the cows, Vidyā, Śivā, the Goddess Maheśvarī; the younger sister of Nārāyaṇa, adorned with humility, whose majesty is praised. (9) The three-eyed one, possessing three crests, the refuge of Śambhu, adorned by the moon; holding a trident in her hand, the upholder of the Vedas, the bestower of auspiciousness, she of auspicious form. (10) Umā, the Blessed Lady, Night, she whose eyes are the moon, sun, and fire; whose earrings embody the nature of the moon and sun, whose pair of breasts are the moon and sun. (11) Ambā, Ambikā, the bearer of the lotus, whose form is water, the nourisher, the steadfast one.

She who is beloved by Śiva, who dwells upon the lap of Śiva, the beautiful one, the destroyer of Śumbha; she who holds a sword in her hand, who is mounted on a bird, who bears a shield, whose form has the luster of the sky; she who wears saffron-colored garments, who is fond of saffron, whose teeth resemble jasmine flowers. She who is Kālī, the bearer of a skull, the fierce one, who holds a scimitar in her hand, and who is Action itself; she who is desirable, the maiden, the crooked one, the mother of Kumāra, and the sovereign of the Kula. She who is Mṛḍānī, whose eyes are like those of a young fawn, whose body is soft, and who is fond of deer; she who was worshipped by Mṛkaṇḍu, who is fond of honey-wine, and who is praised by the assembly of Mothers.

She is the Mother (Mātṛkā), the vine of spring (Mādhavī), whose mind is intoxicated with joy, and whose eyes are like wine; she is the embodiment of bliss, the bestower of delight, the object of meditation for sages, and the one who transcends the mind (Manonmanī). (16) She dwells upon the mountain, is worshipped on sacred festival days, and is the giver of the supreme goal; she is higher than the highest, consisting of pure self-awareness (Parāmarśamayi), and has matured into all things. (17) She is served by those bound by fetters (Pāśi), is beloved by the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati), and is praised by the cattle and the bull; she is the visionary state (Paśyantī), the form of supreme consciousness, the remover of slander, and the Supreme (Parā). (18) She is omniscient, possesses every form, is the ultimate attainment, and is exalted by her riches; she wards off calamities, is easily accessible to her devotees, and is composed of compassion.

19–21. She who possesses all arts (*kalāvatī*), whose root is the arts, whose form is adorned with arts; she who is served by the hosts (*gaṇa*), the mistress of the hosts, the refuge, and free from movement; the sovereign lady (*īśvarī*), the beloved of the Lord (*Īśāna*), the Power (*śakti*) that quells sins; she who dwells in the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), whose nature is the pedestal, who is worshipped by the dappled deer (*pṛṣat*), and who consists of radiance; the great illusion (*mahāmāyā*), the beloved of Mataṅga, the light beyond the worlds (*lokāloka*), the consort of Śiva. **The Declaration of the Fruit:** 22. O Rāma! This most rare hymn of Gaurī, consisting of one hundred and eight names, which is exceedingly beautiful, has been declared to you.

It is like a very firm raft for crossing the ocean of calamities. For those who recite this constantly, misfortunes go far away. It generates the grace of Gaurī and bestows self-knowledge upon men. For those men who recite it with devotion, every desired object is accomplished. In the end, they attain liberation (kaivalya); this which has been spoken by Bhārgava is the truth.
